Senses.Explanation: To have one’s eyes exchanged is to undergo a reversal in which the supposed observer loses command of seeing. Chan case critics use the grotesque image when a word, gesture, or opponent covertly replaces a person’s eye and leaves that person deceived or reoriented. Huanglong Huinan says that penetrating straight through the skull has already exchanged the eyes. Baiyan Fu says both the gandharva king and the Buddha have their eyes exchanged by the other party. An identified Fahua master warns that even a foreign shipmaster would have to exchange his eyes. A source-record speaker says Nansen, Zhaozhou, and the hermit exchange the eyes of anyone whose eye of the Way is unclear.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: The eye is not merely injured but replaced: the verdict marks a case in which apparent mastery of vision changes hands.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The phrase does not say that every change of view is deception; the local appraisal identifies who performs the exchange and who loses visual command.

DifferentThingTest.Reason: The case verdict depends on the single bodily image of replacement and consistently predicates it of a deceived or overturned observer.

DraftEvidence.AliasRationale: Probes preserve eyes, replacement, reversal, and deception without converting the image into a general theory of perception.

ModifierControls.Finding: 換却 presents the original eye as removed and another substituted, stronger than merely opening or blinding it.

FamilyControls.Finding: Having the eyes blinded, not exchanged.
The crown eye as discernment, not a reversal.
Having the nostrils pierced and being led; often paired with loss of control.
The eye of the Way whose clarity determines whether the exchange succeeds.
